text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a performance profile is most useful when it identifies:
options: Only the athlete's best score without context
A rank compared with peers but no test purpose
Strengths, weaknesses, limits, and priorities
A list of results without action priorities
explanation: Profiling should connect valid measurements to performance priorities and practical decisions.

text: A 100-m sprinter's profile shows 10-m acceleration below the team reference, normal maximal-velocity split, and a 12% unilateral jump asymmetry. Which priority is most defensible?
options: Increase sprint volume without checking recovery or asymmetry
Replace the profile with body mass as the training guide
Use the season-best sprint and ignore the asymmetry
Prioritize acceleration and unilateral strength, then retest
explanation: The profile should turn several valid findings into a prioritized, testable intervention rather than an isolated score or an unverified training increase.

text: A football midfielder records a normal countermovement jump but a low Yo-Yo intermittent-recovery result across two standardized tests. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Diagnose cardiac disease from this field result
Assume energy systems are adequate from jump data
Target high-intensity endurance; confirm with retesting
Dismiss the result because field tests inform no training
explanation: A repeated, appropriately administered result can identify a performance quality to investigate, but it does not establish a medical diagnosis.

text: A swimmer's profile shows a stable 50-m time, worsening repeated-sprint recovery, and unchanged body mass over four weeks. What should the profile help the staff decide?
options: Treat body mass as the sole intervention target
Treat one stable time as proof of an optimal programme
Stop all testing until the competition season ends
Review recovery capacity and training distribution
explanation: A profile is useful when related trends inform a practical priority; a stable headline time does not exclude a recovery or training-distribution issue.

text: A rugby back's monitoring profile shows a squad-median 30-m time, a large repeated-sprint decrement, and hip-strength asymmetry. Which output best supports planning?
options: Prioritize extra speed work because the 30-m time is squad-median
Interpret the 30-m rank alongside fatigue, asymmetry, and rugby demands
List results without priorities or follow-up measures for training
Treat the athlete's best sprint score as the complete profile and plan
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: After a six-week block, a junior swimmer has stable 200-m pace, lower stroke-rate efficiency, and shoulder-endurance fatigue late in sets. What should the profile identify?
options: Interpret the 200-m time without technique or fatigue information
Compare peers without recording the swimmer's testing conditions
Link pace, stroke efficiency, and shoulder endurance to next steps
List results without identifying an intervention priority for the swimmer
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: Video review shows a volleyball player's jump height is unchanged, but landing control and repeated-jump height worsen late in practice. The profile should guide:
options: Use jump height without reviewing landing or fatigue patterns
Rank the player without considering repeated-jump performance
List the results without a follow-up decision or training priority
Link landing control and late-set jump loss to targeted training
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A para-athlete's sprint time improves after the start command and assistive setup change from baseline. Before using the result, the profile should first:
options: Accept the faster time despite changed start and equipment
Apply a peer norm without considering assistive equipment
Verify comparable setup before interpreting the faster sprint
Report the result without documenting whether trials match
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: Mid-season data show a rower's lactate-threshold pace improving while peak power declines. How should the performance profile present this pattern?
options: Use the endurance score as the whole performance profile
Rank the rower without checking whether pace and power differ
Report both changes without assigning follow-up priorities
Separate improved threshold pace from reduced peak-power capacity
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: After a rapid weight-management phase, a wrestler has stable body mass, lower grip endurance, and slower reaction time. The best summary is:
options: Infer a diagnosis from grip and reaction results alone
Treat stable body mass as proof that qualities are unchanged
Link weight-management context to grip and reaction priorities
List slower outcomes without a practical next step
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a repeated decline in sprint performance with stable strength may suggest a limitation in:
options: Ferritin status interpreted without other evidence
Validity of every test regardless of protocol and context
Speed power, fatigue tolerance, or sprint technique
Body height as the primary limiting variable
explanation: Performance interpretation compares related qualities and considers fatigue, technique, and sport demands.

text: Across three 400-m trials, a runner's final 100-m split slows progressively while maximal isometric force remains stable. Which quality should be investigated first?
options: Use body height as the main performance explanation
Reject the split data because maximal force was stable
Diagnose iron deficiency from split times alone
Investigate speed endurance and fatigue tolerance
explanation: A late-race slowdown with stable maximal force points toward event-specific speed endurance or fatigue tolerance, while medical causes require separate evidence.

text: A soccer player's 5-m sprint time is normal after 48 hours of rest but 8% slower after two congested match days. What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: Assume a permanent loss of acceleration capacity
Consider residual fatigue before changing technique
Discard the rested result as less relevant
Treat body height as the main determinant of sprint time
explanation: A context-dependent decline after congested competition should first be interpreted with recovery and load information rather than as a permanent technical loss.

text: Video from a sprint test shows longer ground-contact time and reduced front-side mechanics, while force-plate peak force is unchanged. Which limitation is most plausible?
options: Remove technical drills from the programme
Diagnose iron deficiency from video alone
Blame the device despite normal calibration
Investigate sprint technique and coordination
explanation: When peak force is stable but movement mechanics change, technique and coordination are reasonable performance hypotheses to test with targeted analysis.

text: Across three high-load sessions, a sprinter's squat strength remains stable while 30-m acceleration slows. Which quality should be investigated first?
options: Use body size as the primary explanation for slower acceleration without context
Use maximal force without considering sprint demands, context, or fatigue
Infer a medical diagnosis from one performance change without clinical evidence
Investigate fatigue tolerance and sprint technique after repeated high-load sessions
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: During a stage race, a cyclist maintains peak isometric force while five-minute power declines. What should the staff review?
options: Infer a diagnosis from one declining power result without other evidence
Treat isometric force as the complete measure of cycling performance
Review fatigue tolerance and power maintenance across stage-race efforts
Use body mass as the main explanation for a stage-race power decline
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: After four repeated basketball sets, maximal force is unchanged but jump height falls. Which performance quality deserves investigation?
options: Investigate repeated-set power maintenance and jump technique
Use maximal force alone to explain repeated-set jump performance
Infer a diagnosis from lower jump height without other evidence
Blame body size for late-set decline without reviewing fatigue
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: In repeated 100-m swim trials, resisted-pull strength is unchanged but pace fades over the final 25 m. What should be examined?
options: Examine speed endurance and technique during the final 25 metres
Treat resisted-pull strength as the only determinant of 100-m pace
Infer a medical diagnosis from repeated-trial pacing alone
Use body size as the main explanation for late-trial slowdown
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: Following three matches in one week, a footballer retains maximal force but slows during reactive changes of direction. Which interpretation is safest?
options: Treat maximal force as sufficient evidence of readiness for cutting
Assess fatigue tolerance and cutting technique after congested competition
Infer a diagnosis from one post-congestion result without clinical evidence
Use body size as the main explanation for slower direction changes
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: During repeated 2,000-m ergometer efforts, a rower's peak stroke force stays stable while the final 500-m split worsens. Which quality should be prioritized?
options: Treat peak stroke force as the complete measure of 2,000-m performance
Prioritize speed endurance and technique during the final 500 metres
Infer a medical diagnosis from split data without clinical evidence
Use body mass as the primary explanation for the worsening final split
explanation: Stable peak force with a worsening final-500-m split suggests a problem with speed endurance or fatigue tolerance and may also reflect task-specific technique; it does not by itself establish a medical diagnosis.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, when a test result is below a reference value, the first step should be to:
options: Check test quality, context, and reference-group relevance
Treat the score as diagnostic without clinical context
Prescribe maximal training before confirming context
Discard the result because reference groups vary
explanation: A low score requires checking validity, reliability, comparability, and the athlete's context before action.

text: An athlete's countermovement-jump score is 8 cm below a published reference, but testing followed a 90-minute practice and the reference group was tested rested. What should happen first?
options: Label the athlete below standard and add jumps
Discard the reference because norms are unhelpful
Check comparability; repeat under standard conditions
Diagnose fatigue from one post-practice comparison
explanation: Reference comparisons are meaningful only when the test protocol, athlete context, and reference group are sufficiently comparable; standardization should precede a training decision.

text: A 16-year-old gymnast's handgrip value falls below an adult reference table, although age, sex, body mass, and device protocol differ. The first step is to:
options: Apply the adult cut-off as a clinical diagnosis
Verify an age- and protocol-matched reference first
Select whichever reference has the lowest threshold
Replace the measure with a coach's visual impression
explanation: Normative interpretation requires an appropriate reference population and comparable measurement conditions; an adult cut-off should not be applied automatically to a youth athlete.

text: A GPS report shows unusually low high-speed distance in a match, and the device recorded satellite drop-out for 11 minutes. What is the first analytic step?
options: Verify data completeness, device function, and protocol
Increase high-speed workload before verifying the record
Treat missing distance as evidence of poor conditioning
Compare devices without documenting their differences
explanation: A known tracking gap makes data quality and completeness the first issue; the performance value should not drive training until the measurement is verified.

text: A 16-year-old footballer's hamstring strength is 15% below an under-18 reference. Before changing training, what should the clinician check first?
options: Treat the low score as a diagnosis before checking the test
Verify protocol, context, and reference-group comparability
Prescribe maximal loading before confirming measurement and context
Discard the result simply because reference groups can differ
explanation: A result below a reference requires attention to test quality, protocol, reference-group relevance, and athlete context before action.

text: A 400-m specialist falls below a VO2 reference drawn from mixed endurance athletes. What is the best first step?
options: Discard the result because the reference includes other endurance athletes
Treat the low value as disease evidence without further assessment
Prescribe maximal endurance loading before confirming test conditions
Check whether the VO2 protocol and reference group fit the 400-m event
explanation: A result below a reference requires attention to test quality, protocol, reference-group relevance, and athlete context before action.

text: A growing basketball player scores below an age-based jump norm, but maturation and landing surface were not recorded. What should happen first?
options: Record maturation and surface before applying the age-based jump norm
Treat the low score as a diagnosis without considering growth
Prescribe maximal plyometrics before verifying maturation
Discard the score because age norms are never useful for athletes
explanation: A result below a reference requires attention to test quality, protocol, reference-group relevance, and athlete context before action.

text: At the first post-ACL hop session, an athlete falls below a symmetry criterion and reports apprehension. What should the clinician do first?
options: Treat the first low score as proof that progression is unsafe without review
Standardize familiarization and consider apprehension before the criterion
Prescribe maximal hopping before confirming technique, confidence, and symptoms
Discard the result because hop criteria cannot inform rehabilitation
explanation: A result below a reference requires attention to test quality, protocol, reference-group relevance, and athlete context before action.

text: A coach compares a slower field sprint with a laboratory result even though warm-up, start command, and timing system differ. What should be checked first?
options: Treat the slower field time as a definitive speed loss without protocol review
Reconcile protocols, start command, timing system, and reference conditions
Prescribe extra sprint work before confirming comparable measures
Discard the field result because laboratory and field tests cannot be compared
explanation: A result below a reference requires attention to test quality, protocol, reference-group relevance, and athlete context before action.

text: Two days before a final, travel is followed by a repeated-sprint score below reference. What is the most defensible first step?
options: Check travel, protocol, and reference context before judging readiness
Treat the low score as inadequate conditioning without checking recovery
Prescribe maximal sprints before assessing recovery and travel effects
Discard the score because a reference cannot inform pre-final readiness
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a practical training recommendation should link the observed result to:
options: A change without a defined follow-up measure
A feasible intervention linked to a follow-up measure
Only the athlete's ranking without a decision plan
A generic exercise list without athlete-specific goals
explanation: Applied analysis is useful when it produces an actionable intervention and a way to evaluate response.

text: An athlete's isokinetic knee-extension strength is 14% lower on the previously injured side, while the return-to-sport criterion is 10%. A practical recommendation should first:
options: Ignore the asymmetry because the athlete reports no pain
Remove all lower-limb loading until symmetry is perfect
Add targeted strength work and schedule a standardized retest
Use the opposite limb as the only training target
explanation: A meaningful side-to-side deficit should be linked to a proportionate intervention and a predefined reassessment, not ignored or treated as a reason for indefinite unloading.

text: Repeated-sprint testing shows a 6% performance decrement after a congested week, exceeding the athlete's typical error. Which recommendation best links data to action?
options: Adjust high-intensity load and retest after recovery
Declare the athlete unfit for the season from one test
Increase sprint volume to overcome the weekly decrement
Replace sprint testing with a body-mass measure
explanation: A change exceeding expected error can support a proportionate load or recovery adjustment followed by repeat measurement.

text: Video analysis identifies excessive knee valgus on landing in 3 of 5 trials, with stable jump height. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
options: Avoid jumping permanently without measuring response
Use neuromuscular technique work with a landing retest
Use team ranking as the only programme guide
Treat stable jump height as proof landing is normal
explanation: A movement-quality finding should lead to a targeted, feasible intervention and a defined reassessment rather than reliance on jump height alone.

text: Landing video from a volleyball block shows delayed trunk control despite normal jump height. How should the finding be linked to follow-up?
options: Prescribe landing-control work with a trunk-motion reassessment
Add generic exercises without a landing-control goal or measure
Label the video finding as a diagnosis without further assessment
Change training volume without defining how control will be reassessed
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: Following a hard microcycle, a swimmer's shoulder-endurance score falls without pain and maximal pull strength is unchanged. What plan is most appropriate?
options: Use a targeted endurance plan and repeat testing after recovery
Give generic shoulder exercises without a defined endurance target
Diagnose pathology from one post-load decline without clinical findings
Change the programme without setting a reassessment criterion
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: After a congested week, a distance runner has a higher heart rate at the same submaximal pace. What recommendation is most appropriate?
options: Change intensity without defining when the response will be reassessed
Add generic conditioning without a defined recovery or performance target
Diagnose illness from one heart-rate response without other clinical evidence
Review recovery, adjust endurance training, and repeat the submaximal test
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: A rower's peak power is 8% below target while technique remains consistent across trials. What practical recommendation follows?
options: Add unrelated exercises without connecting them to the power deficit
Set a power-focused intervention and retest under the same rowing protocol
Diagnose a physiological disorder from one below-target result alone
Change the programme without defining a power reassessment or threshold
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: Cutting video shows excessive trunk sway in a footballer who has normal straight-line speed. What should be recommended?
options: Increase running volume without defining how cutting control will be checked
Prescribe general conditioning without a braking-control objective
Diagnose a movement disorder from one video observation alone
Use braking-control drills and reassess trunk sway during comparable cuts
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: A climber preparing for a route has below-demand timed-hang capacity but normal maximal grip force. What is the best plan?
options: Add exercises without linking them to timed-hang demand or reassessment
Target finger-flexor endurance and repeat a route-specific hang test
Change route selection without addressing the measured endurance deficit
Diagnose a climbing disorder from one below-demand result without review
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, longitudinal monitoring is strengthened by using:
options: Only the best result from each testing period
Different tests each session without common timing
Consistent measures, repeated timing, trends, and context
Informal impressions without recorded measurements
explanation: Repeated standardized measurement makes trends more interpretable than isolated observations.

text: Over six weeks, countermovement jumps were recorded on different devices and at different times relative to training. To strengthen the longitudinal comparison, the staff should:
options: Standardize device, timing, warm-up, and recording
Convert scores to team ranks and discard raw values
Average scores without recording testing conditions
Select the best weekly value to represent potential
explanation: Consistent device, timing, preparation, and recording conditions make repeated scores more interpretable as a trend.

text: A wellness questionnaire used a 1–5 fatigue scale for four weeks and then changed to 1–10 without an overlap study. What is the main monitoring problem?
options: Re-establish comparability before interpreting later scores
Treat the change as evidence of greater fatigue
Discard all subjective data from the first four weeks
Assume the new scale automatically improves validity
explanation: Changing the response scale interrupts comparability; the new scale needs a documented bridge or a new baseline before trends are interpreted.

text: One athlete's GPS high-speed distance was collected with two device models using different sampling settings. A defensible longitudinal analysis should:
options: Pool device values because both report metres
Use the largest distance to avoid underestimation
Document settings and compare compatible periods
Replace missing metadata with the team mean
explanation: Device and sampling differences can affect measured distances, so metadata and compatible periods must be considered before combining a time series.

text: A readiness programme uses a different jump device, warm-up, and timing procedure at every session. How should monitoring be improved?
options: Allow different devices, warm-ups, and timing across readiness sessions
Choose only each athlete's highest score without a common protocol
Keep the device, warm-up, timing, and instructions consistent
Replace recorded measures with informal staff impressions
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A developing athlete grows 4 cm while standing-long-jump distance improves. What information is needed to interpret the trend?
options: Ignore growth because distance is the only relevant result for this athlete
Record growth, surface, timing, and the same protocol at each assessment
Replace measurements with a coach's impression of development
Select the longest jump without considering maturation or conditions
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A team measures readiness during a congested fixture period. Which testing design gives the strongest comparison?
options: Keep test timing, warm-up, device, and match-day context consistent
Use each athlete's best result as the readiness baseline without standardization
Rely on staff impressions when the fixture schedule becomes busy for decisions
Test whenever convenient without recording match timing or context
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: At week six of ACL rehabilitation, hop distance has been measured with changing instructions. What should be done before comparing scores?
options: Compare distances despite changing instructions, surface, and landing criteria
Replace hop measurements with an informal confidence rating and no criteria
Use the longest hop as a baseline without checking technique or symptoms
Standardize instructions, surface, limb order, and familiarization
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A six-week monitoring file contains laboratory force tests and field jump tests. What should be documented for interpretation?
options: Document each test's protocol, timing, equipment, units, and context
Use one combined score despite different units, protocols, and purposes
Use only the largest change as evidence of progress without protocol context
Replace repeated measurements with staff impressions and no records
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: The day before a swimmer's major final, how should readiness be compared with the athlete's baseline?
options: Use a different warm-up, time, or start procedure before the final
Replace testing with a documented coach impression before the final
Select the best historical result without matching test conditions
Repeat the baseline protocol at a similar time using the same instructions
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a small change in an athlete's score should be considered practically important only when it:
options: Improves the athlete's rank by one place in the sample
Exceeds expected error or changes the practical decision
Adds decimal places without improving measurement precision
Is numerically nonzero but below the decision threshold
explanation: Statistical or numerical change is not automatically practically important; error and decision relevance matter.

text: A sprinter improves from 10.20 s to 10.18 s, but the test's typical error is 0.04 s and no coaching decision would change. The change should be interpreted as:
options: Treat it as unclear because it is below typical error
Call the lower time a meaningful gain immediately
Assume the timing test has perfect reliability
Remove timing error from the performance record
explanation: A numerical difference smaller than expected measurement error is not clearly a real or decision-relevant performance change.

text: An athlete's jump height increases 5 cm, exceeding the test's typical error of 2 cm and crossing the programme's return-to-training threshold. This change is practically important because it:
options: Call any nonzero change practically important
Use peer rank even when the protocol changed
Treat extra decimal places as evidence of improvement
Exceeds error and changes the decision
explanation: The change is more credible than expected error and is large enough to alter the predefined practical decision.

text: A study reports p=0.03 for a 0.02-second sprint improvement, but the 95% confidence interval includes values smaller than the timing error. What should guide the practical interpretation?
options: Treat p<0.05 alone as proof of a useful change
Consider effect size, uncertainty, error, and decisions
Ignore inference because sport measurements vary
Replace the confidence interval with athlete ranking
explanation: Practical interpretation combines effect magnitude and uncertainty with measurement error and the decision threshold; a p value alone is insufficient.

text: A timing-gate sprint improves by 0.02 s, but the change is smaller than the system's timing error. When could it be practically important?
options: Change ranking despite a result within normal timing error
Treat a nonzero result below threshold as important
Add decimal places without improving measurement precision
Exceed timing error or change a predefined performance decision
explanation: Because the improvement is smaller than timing error, it is not clearly beyond measurement noise; it becomes practically relevant only if it exceeds error or changes a predefined decision.

text: A resistance test rises by 1 kg while familiarization variation is 2 kg. How should the apparent change be interpreted?
options: Call it a gain because the measured value increased on one trial
Change training without repeating the test or reviewing familiarization
Call it a precise result because the scale records kilograms
Require it to exceed familiarization error or change a loading decision
explanation: The 1-kg increase is smaller than the 2-kg familiarization variation, so it should not be treated as a dependable gain unless it exceeds that error or changes a justified loading decision.

text: A daily wellness score rises from 6 to 7 on a scale with three-point day-to-day variation. What is the responsible conclusion?
options: Call it meaningful only beyond expected variation or a preset threshold
Treat one point as proof of recovery despite scale variation
Add decimal places without addressing day-to-day scale variation
Change training after any nonzero wellness difference or isolated response
explanation: A one-point wellness increase is smaller than the scale's three-point day-to-day variation, so it is meaningful only if it exceeds expected variation or a preset threshold.

text: A jump-height change exceeds typical error and crosses the team's smallest worthwhile change. What can the result support?
options: Dismiss it because no jump test is perfectly reliable or decision-relevant
Use it for a decision when protocol and context are comparable
Treat it as proof that every performance quality improved after the test
Replace recovery information with the jump result without checking context
explanation: Exceeding typical error and the smallest worthwhile change supports using the jump result in a decision when protocol and athlete context remain comparable.

text: Repeated limb tests show asymmetry moving from 8% to 7%, while trial variation is 3%. How should the change be interpreted?
options: Call it clinical improvement because the percentage decreased on retest
Change rehabilitation without repeating the asymmetry test
Call any percentage change clinically important without considering error
Judge the small change against error and a decision threshold
explanation: The one-percentage-point asymmetry change is smaller than the 3% trial variation, so it should be judged against error and a clinically or practically relevant threshold.

text: A blood-lactate value falls by 0.3 mmol/L, less than analytical and biological variation. What should staff conclude?
options: Call it adaptation because the value decreased despite variation
Add decimal places without addressing sampling and biological variation
Consider it meaningful only beyond variation or a decision threshold
Change the programme without checking sampling conditions
explanation: A 0.3-mmol/L lactate decrease below analytical and biological variation is not dependable evidence of adaptation unless it exceeds variation or changes a justified decision.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, when communicating data to a coach, the analyst should emphasize:
options: Every raw variable without interpretation or prioritization
Decision relevance, uncertainty, and practical next step
Only the most favorable result without uncertainty
A causal claim based on one correlation alone
explanation: Good communication translates evidence into a clear decision while preserving uncertainty and limitations.

text: A coach requests all 30 variables from a monitoring dashboard before selecting next week's training. The analyst should first present:
options: Causal claims from the strongest correlation
Every raw variable without decision priorities
Only favorable trends to protect confidence
Key trends, uncertainty, and next steps
explanation: Communication should prioritize decision-relevant findings, their limitations, and an actionable next step rather than overwhelm the decision-maker with unfiltered data.

text: In 12 athletes, weekly training load correlates with injury days (r=0.62), but exposure time and prior injury were not recorded. The coach should be told that:
options: Say the correlation proves load caused injury
Say correlations never help guide coaching
Reduce all training load without further analysis
Describe an association, noting possible confounding
explanation: An unadjusted association with missing exposure and prior-injury information does not establish causation and should be treated as preliminary.

text: An athlete's seven-day HRV average drops 12% while sprint performance is unchanged and sleep reports worsen. The most useful communication is to:
options: Increase training load to test the HRV signal
Report HRV with baseline, sleep, and recovery context
Ignore HRV because sprint performance is unchanged
Diagnose overtraining from the HRV change alone
explanation: A monitoring signal should be interpreted with individual baseline, performance, sleep, and recovery context before a training adjustment is made.

text: A GPS dashboard reports an 8% increase in high-speed running to a coach. What should the analyst emphasize?
options: Report the percentage without defining the metric or baseline
Rank peers without explaining exposure, device, or match context
Define the metric, baseline, uncertainty, and decision it may inform
Diagnose injury or illness from one dashboard value without clinical review
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: An athlete asks why a monitoring score fell after a match. How should the result be explained?
options: Say the score proves recovery has failed without reviewing other indicators
Use peer ranking instead of the athlete's own trend and baseline
Explain its scale, baseline, match context, uncertainty, and next action
Say one score establishes a clinical diagnosis without clinical review
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: A coach wants to compare a goalkeeper's reaction time with a sprinter's. What should be explained first?
options: Assume the lower number is better in both sports
Diagnose a limitation from one reaction-time value
Use peer ranking despite different tasks and test conditions
Define both tasks, protocols, and relevant reference data
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: A runner reports more pain even though weekly running volume is stable. How should this be communicated?
options: Report pain without baseline, running exposure, or symptom context
Rank the athlete without discussing individual context or baseline
Describe pain with baseline, uncertainty, and clinical follow-up
Declare an injury cause from the pain report alone without examination
explanation: Evidence-informed application links the finding to a feasible decision, acknowledges uncertainty, and uses an appropriate follow-up measure.

text: A manager requests a public ranking based on health-related readiness scores. What should the analyst emphasize?
options: Publish individual scores to make the ranking transparent to the whole squad
Compare athletes without defining the health measure or its limits
Protect confidentiality and report aggregated, decision-relevant data
Use one score for selection without clinical review or individual context
explanation: Health-related readiness data should be protected through need-to-know access and aggregated reporting when individual identity is not required for the decision.

text: Two staff members interpret the same workload dashboard differently. How should the disagreement be resolved?
options: Agree on definitions, context, thresholds, and the supported decision
Let both interpretations guide training without clarifying the metric
Choose the interpretation producing the largest training change
Use the dashboard as a diagnosis without discussing uncertainty
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a sudden outlier in a monitoring dashboard should first prompt a check of:
options: An injury diagnosis based on one unusual value
Deletion of the observation without checking context
Data entry, device function, protocol, and athlete context
An immediate training increase without confirming cause
explanation: Outliers may reflect true change or measurement and data-management problems, so they require verification.

text: A force-plate dashboard shows body mass doubled for one athlete on one day, with all other variables unchanged. Before interpreting training status, check:
options: The athlete's motivation score alone
Maximal loading based on the unusual value
Calibration, units, identity, and data records
Silent replacement with the previous value
explanation: An implausible isolated value should first be verified against calibration, units, identity, and data-entry records.

text: A wellness score of 1 appears after an athlete submitted the questionnaire twice, once with a missing date. The first data-quality check should address:
options: Training based on the most extreme response
A diagnosis of severe fatigue from the single score
Deletion of the lower score without an audit trail
Duplicate records, timestamps, and missingness
explanation: Duplicate submissions and missing timestamps can create a false outlier; the records and missingness pattern should be checked before interpretation.

text: GPS sprint distance falls to zero immediately after a firmware update, while the athlete's video shows normal sprinting. The analyst should first:
options: Check firmware, synchronization, and tracking
Increase sprint exposure to correct the value
Treat zero distance as a true loss of speed
Replace the value with a teammate's average
explanation: The timing of the zero value and the independent video evidence make a device or synchronization check necessary before using the metric.

text: One GPS file shows 40% more high-speed distance after a brief loss of satellite lock. What should be checked first?
options: Change training after accepting the value as a true outlier
Verify satellite lock, device quality, processing, protocol, and raw data
Use the value as a baseline before checking the lost signal and protocol
Diagnose performance change from one unconfirmed record without context
explanation: A brief satellite-lock loss can distort GPS distance and speed estimates, so satellite quality, processing, protocol, and raw records should be verified before interpreting performance.

text: A force plate records a sudden 20% jump-height increase immediately after being moved. What should be checked first?
options: Increase plyometric loading because the force-plate result improved
Conclude explosive power changed from one day's result
Replace the new value with the previous best without documenting why
Check calibration, placement, body mass, protocol, and raw traces
explanation: Moving a force plate can affect placement and calibration; body-mass records, protocol, and raw traces should be checked before accepting an abrupt jump-height change.

text: During a hard interval, an optical heart-rate trace is flat while perceived effort is normal. How should the signal be troubleshot?
options: Treat the flat trace as proof the interval was not strenuous without checking effort
Check sensor contact, firmware, signal, protocol, and an independent measure
Delete the trace and report only perceived effort without checking the device
Increase intensity because the device showed no cardiovascular response
explanation: A flat optical heart-rate trace despite normal effort may reflect contact, firmware, signal, or protocol problems, so an independent measure helps verify the recording.

text: A lactate sample is an extreme outlier and was collected 20 minutes late. What should be checked?
options: Check sampling time, analyzer function, units, protocol, and raw record
Redefine lactate threshold immediately from one outlier and late sample
Replace the value with a team average without recording the discrepancy
Diagnose abnormal metabolism from a delayed sample alone
explanation: A sample collected 20 minutes late can produce an invalid lactate comparison; sampling time, analyzer function, units, protocol, and the raw record should be checked first.

text: A wellness score drops sharply after a response entered at an unusual time following a reminder. What should be checked?
options: Check timestamp, duplicates, reminder context, and raw entry
Assume the reminder caused a genuine recovery decline
Change training from one low response before verifying the entry
Delete the low score without documenting the decision
explanation: An unusual response time and reminder context can affect a wellness entry, so timestamps, duplicate submissions, and the raw response should be checked before changing training.

text: A timing gate records a sprint far slower than video and the athlete's next trial. What should be reviewed?
options: Treat the slow gate time as a true loss of sprint capacity
Replace it with the next trial without checking the first record
Add sprint volume because the isolated time suggests poor fitness
Check gate setup, timing data, start procedure, and video
explanation: A gate time that conflicts with video and the next trial warrants checking setup, start procedure, timing data, and video before inferring a capacity loss.

text: If an athlete's performance improves while training load also rises, the safest interpretation is:
options: The athlete cannot be fatigued because performance improved
Higher load is always beneficial when performance improves
Consider response alongside recovery, trends, and other outcomes
The result proves the programme is optimal for the athlete
explanation: A single favorable outcome does not establish causality or eliminate the need to monitor recovery and risk.

text: During a two-week congested schedule, external load rises 20%, sprint performance improves 3%, but sleep and wellness scores deteriorate. The safest interpretation is:
options: Interpret performance with recovery and illness-risk indicators
Assume the load is beneficial because performance improved
Assume fatigue is impossible when sprint performance rises
Ignore wellness scores because they are subjective
explanation: A favorable performance result does not remove concern from worsening recovery indicators; the combined pattern should inform progression.

text: Two athletes complete the same weekly load; one improves sprint performance and the other declines with poor sleep. What conclusion is most defensible?
options: Consider individual response and recovery
Treat the declining athlete's result as invalid
Assume both athletes had the same physiological response
Use the improving athlete to clear the whole squad
explanation: The same external load can produce different responses, so individual recovery and performance trends should inform interpretation.

text: An athlete's performance improves during a planned taper while training load falls. Which interpretation is most cautious?
options: Attribute improvement to the previous high load alone
Treat the pre-taper score as invalid without checking conditions
Keep future load minimal after any taper improvement
Judge the taper with planned load, recovery, and trends
explanation: Improvement during a taper is compatible with several explanations; planned load, recovery, and repeated trends are needed before attributing causality.

text: Over six weeks, a soccer team raises weekly load 15% and improves repeated-sprint score 3%. What is the safest conclusion?
options: Compare the gain with recovery, match exposure, and other outcomes
Increase load again because one performance measure improved
Assume the load increase alone caused the performance gain over six weeks
Stop monitoring because the repeated-sprint score improved
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: After resisted runs and higher volume, a sprinter improves acceleration. Before adding more volume, what should be determined?
options: Credit resisted runs alone despite other training changes and recovery
Check recovery, technique, prior trend, and training dose before progressing
Add volume because acceleration improved once without checking fatigue
Stop monitoring because the latest acceleration time was faster
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A jumper's power improves while load rises, but sleep and morning readiness worsen for ten days. How should the pattern be interpreted?
options: Balance improved power against deteriorating recovery indicators
Add load because power improved without reviewing sleep or fatigue
Call rising load beneficial because power is higher despite poor recovery
Ignore sleep and readiness when performance improves over repeated sessions
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: During late-stage rehabilitation, a footballer improves hop symmetry after increasing running load but still has cutting pain. How should the data be used?
options: Clear unrestricted cutting because hop symmetry normalized without checking pain
Combine hop symmetry, pain, and cutting function in a graded progression
Increase running and cutting because one measure improved without reviewing pain
Stop monitoring because the rehabilitation score improved and pain was reported
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A cyclist's five-minute power improves during a period of shortened sleep. What is the safest interpretation?
options: Interpret power with sleep, fatigue, repeated tests, and context
Increase load because power is better without checking fatigue
Attribute the gain to training without checking sleep or other conditions
Treat sleep as irrelevant because performance improved on one test
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A swimmer's race pace improves after a large interval-volume increase, but persistent soreness is reported. What conclusion is appropriate?
options: Repeat intervals because race pace improved despite soreness and fatigue
Add volume because race pace improved without reviewing soreness or recovery
Consider pace, soreness, recovery, and risk before adding volume
Stop monitoring because race pace improved in one favorable test
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a useful performance dashboard should avoid:
options: Displaying a small set of metrics with documented definitions and context
Displaying athlete scores alongside dates and relevant reference ranges
Displaying metrics without definitions, context, or a decision purpose
Displaying trends with clear units, dates, and a defined decision purpose
explanation: Dashboards support decisions when measures are defined, contextualized, and connected to action.

text: A dashboard for a squad displays 40 metrics, mixed units, no definitions, and no stated decisions. Its main weakness is that it:
options: Assuming squad trends are never useful
Presenting measures without context or purpose
Rejecting quantitative data for coach observation
Avoiding more than one outcome per screen
explanation: A dashboard becomes less useful when measures lack definitions, units, context, and a clear decision purpose.

text: A performance dashboard shows injury status, GPS location, and athlete names on a screen visible to visitors. What should the analyst avoid?
options: Use dates and units to interpret performance trends
Restrict access and show only decision-relevant information
Explain every metric to the authorized performance team
Display identifiable health and location data to visitors
explanation: Identifiable health and location information should not be exposed to unauthorized viewers; access and presentation should be limited to the decision need.

text: A dashboard reports a 12% improvement in jump height but omits baseline value, test error, and timing conditions. It should avoid:
options: Interpreting percentage change without baseline or test context
Displaying a non-health performance result beside a name
Graphing repeated measurements across the testing period
Linking the trend to a clearly defined coaching decision
explanation: The dashboard should avoid interpreting percentage change without baseline, uncertainty, and test-protocol context.

text: A dashboard designer combines sprint time, wellness, and injury status into one unlabelled colour score. What should be avoided?
options: Display dated sprint, wellness, and injury measures with separate labels
Use an unlabelled composite hiding performance and health measures
Define how each component was collected in a protocol note
Set a follow-up rule linked to the combined data and decision
explanation: An unlabelled composite can hide distinct performance and health constructs, so the component measures should remain separately labelled and interpretable.

text: A squad dashboard ranks athletes by one jump score without showing test error or reference context. What should be avoided?
options: Show a dated trend with a preplanned retest threshold and context
Separate individual change from peer comparison and reference context
Use an isolated rank without test error or reference context
Display the score with its protocol and uncertainty noted
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: An automated alert fires after one abnormal recovery score from an incomplete entry made after travel. What should be avoided?
options: Send a provisional alert for confirmation before staff action
Review repeated patterns with travel and response-quality context
Link a confirmed abnormal pattern to a defined follow-up plan
Use an unverified outlier to change training after one response
explanation: Performance interpretation should integrate valid measures, test context, fatigue, technique, and sport demands rather than overread an isolated score.

text: A dashboard displays 35 metrics but links none of them to a staff decision. What should be avoided?
options: Organize measures around coaching questions and actions
Show units, dates, protocols, and decision context for each measure
Display many metrics without linking them to a staff decision
Assign follow-up to meaningful changes in a review process
explanation: Metrics are more useful when linked to a defined coaching question or decision; displaying many unconnected measures increases noise without guiding action.

text: A screen visible to all athletes displays identifiable illness and pain scores. What should be avoided?
options: Use aggregate health trends when individual identity is unnecessary
Restrict access according to the monitoring purpose and role
Display identifiable health data without a need to know
Record which authorized staff accessed sensitive reports
explanation: Identifiable health data should be restricted to authorized staff with a legitimate need to know, with aggregate reporting used when individual identity is unnecessary.

text: A wellness chart combines responses collected before training on some days and after training on others. What should be avoided?
options: Label collection timing beside every wellness observation and trend
Use a trendline that ignores pre- or post-training timing
Separate pre-training and post-training responses in the plot
Document match, travel, and collection context beside the trend
explanation: Mixing pre-training and post-training wellness observations can create a misleading trend, so collection timing must be separated or labelled before comparison.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a randomized controlled trial is designed primarily to compare:
options: Naturally occurring groups without allocating an intervention to participants
Outcomes under allocated interventions while reducing confounding
A single athlete's trend without a comparison condition or allocation
A measurement device's calibration across repeated technical trials
explanation: Random allocation can reduce systematic baseline differences when evaluating an intervention.

text: A six-week hamstring-prevention trial randomizes athletes to two programmes, but 18% withdraw from one group. Which appraisal question is most important before interpreting the result?
options: Ask whether the paper uses a sports-specific font
Ask whether participants trained at the same venue
Check whether differential withdrawals biased analysis
Ask whether the trial measured several outcomes
explanation: Differential withdrawal can bias the comparison, so the analysis population and handling of missing outcomes must be examined before interpreting the randomized trial.

text: In an RCT of two recovery protocols, baseline sleep differs by chance between groups. The most appropriate report should:
options: Report outcomes with uncertainty and discuss the imbalance
Hide baseline differences because randomization balances groups
Change the design to a cohort after seeing baseline data
Compare only the best responder from each study group
explanation: Randomization reduces systematic imbalance but does not guarantee identical baseline values; transparent reporting and uncertainty are essential.

text: A randomized study compares a neuromuscular programme with usual training, but the intervention group also receives extra staff contact. The main design concern is:
options: Claiming no outcome because staff contact is unmeasured
Claiming randomization fails when programmes are visible
Treating extra staff contact as a possible co-intervention
Removing the control group because the intervention is promising
explanation: Unequal staff contact is a co-intervention that may partly explain the outcome difference, complicating attribution to the neuromuscular programme.

text: In a rehabilitation trial, injured athletes are randomly allocated to two programmes and return-to-running time is compared. What does the design compare?
options: Compare return-to-running outcomes under assigned programmes
Use one participant's change without a comparison group
Use self-selected programmes without accounting for baseline
Check repeatability of the timing device under the same protocol
explanation: Random allocation creates assigned programmes that can be compared through the difference in return-to-running outcomes, subject to adherence and uncertainty.

text: In a cycling nutrition trial, athletes are randomly assigned carbohydrate or placebo drinks before testing. What does the design compare?
options: Compare cycling outcomes under assigned carbohydrate and placebo drinks
Compare one athlete's trend without a placebo, allocation, or control group
Compare athletes who chose their own drink and training strategy
Check repeatability of core-temperature measurement across trials
explanation: Randomly assigned carbohydrate and placebo groups provide the intervention contrast used to compare cycling-test outcomes.

text: An eight-week swim trial randomly assigns athletes to technique training or usual training. What does the design estimate?
options: Compare natural differences among swimmers choosing programmes without allocation
Compare one swimmer's change without a control or usual-training condition
Check repeatability of the eight-week outcome test under the protocol
Estimate the contrast between assigned technique training and usual training
explanation: Random allocation permits estimation of the outcome contrast between assigned technique training and usual training, rather than a self-selection association.

text: In a post-ACL trial, participants are randomly assigned two exercise doses and outcomes are assessed blindly. What is compared?
options: Compare participants who selected their preferred exercise dose
Compare one participant's progress without a comparator or baseline
Check device repeatability across rehabilitation assessments
Compare assigned exercise-dose outcomes with blinded assessment
explanation: The trial compares outcomes under the two assigned exercise doses; blinded assessment helps reduce outcome-assessment bias but does not change the assigned-group contrast.

text: An endurance experiment randomly assigns two hydration strategies and measures core temperature. What question does it address?
options: Compare hydration habits among athletes choosing their own strategy
Follow one athlete's temperature trend without a comparison strategy
Compare core temperature under two assigned hydration strategies
Check whether the thermometer gives repeatable readings
explanation: Random assignment creates two hydration-strategy groups whose core-temperature outcomes can be contrasted while accounting for uncertainty and adherence.

text: A sleep-coaching trial randomly assigns athletes to coaching or usual routines and measures reaction time. What is the central comparison?
options: Study sleep routines selected by athletes expecting improvement
Follow one reaction-time trend without a usual-routine comparison
Check repeatability of the reaction-time device across standardized trials
Compare reaction time under assigned coaching and usual routines
explanation: The central RCT comparison is reaction time under assigned sleep coaching versus the assigned usual routine, not a self-selected sleep association.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a cohort study commonly follows participants to examine:
options: Associations between exposures and later outcomes
Definition and classification of an athlete's somatotype
Calibration of one laboratory instrument over repeated trials
Reliability of one instrument under repeated conditions
explanation: Cohort studies observe exposure and outcome over time without necessarily assigning an intervention.

text: A prospective cohort records sleep below 7 hours or at least 7 hours at preseason and follows athletes for 10 weeks to record illness. The exposure is:
options: Sleep category recorded before follow-up
Illness days recorded during follow-up
The analyst's recruitment decision
The athlete's final performance ranking
explanation: In this cohort, sleep category is measured before follow-up and is the exposure used to examine a later illness outcome.

text: A cohort study follows athletes with high versus low weekly travel for one season and compares new overuse injuries. This design can estimate:
options: Device reliability without repeated trials
Baseline disease prevalence only
A causal effect after random allocation
The travel–injury association over follow-up
explanation: A prospective cohort can compare subsequent outcome occurrence across naturally observed exposure groups, while causal interpretation remains cautious.

text: Former injury is more common among athletes who use a recovery device, and those athletes also receive more medical contact. In a cohort analysis, medical contact may:
options: Be an outcome that follows device use in every athlete
Remove the need to record when device use occurred
Confound the device–injury association when linked to both
Prove that device use caused each new injury
explanation: A factor related to both exposure and outcome ascertainment can distort an observed association and should be considered in the analysis.

text: A season-long academy cohort records weekly training load and follows players. What relationship does it examine?
options: Assess repeatability of the load monitor across repeated sessions
Estimate a randomized effect of assigned training load on outcomes
Explain every illness or injury event through body type alone
Examine the association between weekly load and later outcomes
explanation: A prospective cohort classifies or records weekly load without random assignment and examines its association with later player outcomes.

text: At preseason, athletes are classified by sleep duration and followed for respiratory illness. What does the cohort examine?
options: Examine the association between baseline sleep and later illness
Estimate a randomized effect of assigned sleep duration
Check whether the sleep instrument gives repeatable scores over time
Claim sleep alone caused every illness without other evidence
explanation: The cohort observes baseline sleep duration and follows athletes for later respiratory illness, estimating an association rather than a randomized effect.

text: A season-long study records travel days without assigning them and later records muscle complaints. What can it estimate?
options: Check repeatability of the travel log across the season
Examine the association between recorded travel and later complaints
Estimate a randomized travel effect after assigning travel exposure
Estimate starting prevalence of muscle complaints before follow-up
explanation: Recorded travel exposure precedes follow-up for muscle complaints, so the design can examine their association but cannot claim a randomized travel effect.

text: A rehabilitation registry groups patients by home-exercise adherence and follows return to running. What does it examine?
options: Check repeatability of home-exercise reports across follow-up
Examine the association between adherence and return-to-running time
Estimate a randomized effect of assigned adherence on recovery
Estimate prevalence without comparing follow-up outcomes between groups
explanation: The registry observes home-exercise adherence and later return-to-running time, estimating an observational association that may be confounded by adherence-related factors.

text: A club cohort follows athletes who do or do not use a recovery room and records illness for four weeks. What does it ask?
options: Check repeatability of the recovery-room record across four weeks
Examine the association between recovery-room use and later illness
Estimate a randomized effect of assigned recovery-room use on illness
Claim the recovery room prevents illness in every athlete
explanation: The cohort compares observed recovery-room use with later illness, so it estimates an association rather than a randomized preventive effect.

text: A university cohort records low-energy-availability indicators and follows runners for bone-stress injury. What does it examine?
options: Check repeatability of the energy-availability indicator
Claim bone-stress injury has no confounding explanation
Estimate a randomized effect of assigned energy availability on injury
Examine the association of baseline indicators with later injury
explanation: Baseline low-energy-availability indicators are followed against later bone-stress injury, allowing an association to be examined without randomizing energy availability.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, critical appraisal of a paper should include assessment of:
options: Only the journal's visual design and presentation style
Methods, bias, precision, applicability, and claim-data fit
Only the number of references cited by the paper
Whether the conclusion sounds confident and persuasive
explanation: Appraisal asks whether the design and analysis support the reported conclusion and whether it applies to the athlete setting.

text: A paper reports a statistically significant 0.03-second sprint improvement after training, but the confidence interval overlaps the test's typical error. Critical appraisal should ask whether the estimate is:
options: Generalizable without examining the sample
Acceptable on the basis of p<0.05 alone
Precise and relevant to the decision
Reliable because of journal impact factor alone
explanation: Statistical significance does not establish practical importance; the estimate's precision, measurement error, and decision threshold must also be considered.

text: A recovery intervention study includes eight national-level athletes from one sport and reports a large effect. To assess applicability, the reader should examine:
options: Acceptance based only on confident wording
Preference based only on the largest reported effect
Fit of sample and setting to the athlete and decision
Assumption that significance removes sampling uncertainty
explanation: Applicability depends on similarity between the study population, setting, intervention, outcome, and the athlete or decision under consideration.

text: An observational paper states that a high acute-to-chronic load ratio causes injury, but load and injury were measured during the same week. Which appraisal issue is most important?
options: Assume identical training histories are necessary
Require random allocation in every observational study
Reject the paper if descriptive statistics are reported
Ask whether temporal order and confounding permit causation
explanation: Simultaneous observational measurement weakens temporal inference; confounding must be considered before an association is described as causal.

text: When appraising a small rehabilitation trial with a large effect and substantial loss to follow-up, what should be considered?
options: Judge journal style without examining study methods, bias, or applicability
Appraise attrition bias, precision, and rehabilitation applicability
Accept a large effect without checking missing outcomes or attrition
Treat statistical direction as benefit without context or uncertainty
explanation: Substantial loss to follow-up can create attrition bias and reduce precision, so the large effect must be judged for missing outcomes and rehabilitation applicability.

text: A single-club wearable study uses an unvalidated fatigue score. What should a reader appraise?
options: Treat the wearable brand as proof of measurement validity
Generalize one club's sample to every athlete and setting
Appraise validation, sampling bias, precision, and applicability
Accept the association without checking score validation or uncertainty
explanation: An unvalidated fatigue score threatens measurement validity, while a single-club sample and imprecision limit how confidently the finding transfers to other athletes.

text: A cohort links high training load to injury but omits prior injury and exposure timing. What should appraisal address?
options: Accept the association without prior-injury and exposure-timing data
Infer causation from the reported p value alone without context
Appraise confounding, timing, measurement quality, and applicability
Assume a strong load effect despite unmeasured confounding
explanation: Omitted prior injury and exposure timing can confound the load–injury association; measurement quality and applicability must also be appraised.

text: A review pools recovery studies with very different protocols and outcomes. What should be appraised?
options: Accept pooled results despite different recovery protocols
Appraise compatibility, heterogeneity, bias, and relevance
Judge the review by citation count instead of methods
Ignore heterogeneity because the overall effect is significant
explanation: Very different protocols and outcomes create heterogeneity and question whether pooling is meaningful, alongside bias and relevance of the review.

text: A paper claims a warm-up prevents hamstring injury but poorly reports its comparator, adherence, and confidence interval. What should be asked?
options: Appraise comparator, adherence, uncertainty, and study design
Accept the warm-up claim because it sounds plausible
Ignore comparator and adherence during interpretation
Ignore confidence intervals because results are positive
explanation: A poorly reported comparator, adherence, and confidence interval weaken interpretation of the warm-up claim and require critical appraisal before application.

text: A wearable paper links daily load to performance but has frequent missing data and one elite squad. What should be appraised?
options: Accept the relationship despite missing data and one-team sampling
Appraise missing data, selection bias, precision, and transferability
Generalize one elite squad to every athlete without qualification
Treat the association as causal without checking missingness
explanation: Frequent missing data and one-team sampling can introduce selection bias and reduce transferability, so precision and missingness must be considered.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, a confounder is a variable that:
options: Is unrelated to exposure and outcome but adds random noise
Is the primary outcome selected before exposure measurement
Is measurement error caused only by an unreliable instrument
Relates to exposure and outcome and distorts their association
explanation: Confounding can create or mask an association when a third variable relates to exposure and outcome.

text: In a study of recovery boots, users have substantially greater training age than non-users, and training age is related to injury risk. Training age may be:
options: Random error unrelated to exposure or outcome
A pressure unit used for the boots
A confounder of boot use and injury
An outcome that follows every injury
explanation: Training age is a plausible confounder when it relates to both recovery-device use and injury risk and is not part of the causal exposure definition.

text: Outdoor training days are associated with both higher heat exposure and more muscle cramps. If heat exposure is not controlled, it may:
options: Leave outcome definition unclear before analysis
Lead to the claim that outdoor training causes cramps
Make the observational cohort appear randomized
Confound the outdoor-training–cramp association
explanation: A third variable related to both the exposure and outcome can distort their observed association if it is not addressed.

text: High-protein diet use is associated with better sprint improvement, but users also receive more individualized coaching. Individualized coaching is a possible confounder because it:
options: Fails to relate diet choice to sprint improvement
Attributes the association to timing error
Influences both diet choice and sprint improvement
Measures the outcome before the dietary exposure
explanation: Individualized coaching may influence both diet choice and sprint improvement, so the diet–performance association may be partly confounded.

text: In a load-injury analysis, previously injured athletes receive modified loads and have higher injury risk. What role does previous injury play?
options: Random error unrelated to training load and injury
An outcome definition selected after seeing the injury results
A report detail unrelated to either study variable
A variable related to both modified load and injury risk
explanation: A confounder is related to both the exposure and outcome and can distort their observed association.

text: An analyst studies the association between travel, poor sleep, and illness. What kind of variable could confound it?
options: A variable unrelated to both travel and illness outcomes
A factor associated with travel and illness before both occur
A post-analysis outcome definition unrelated to both variables
A timing error affecting only the sleep questionnaire
explanation: A confounder is related to both the exposure and outcome and can distort their observed association.

text: A supplement study finds higher power in users, but stronger athletes are more likely to choose supplements. What is the confounder?
options: Random error unrelated to supplement use, strength, or power
A post-hoc outcome definition chosen after reviewing power results
A report detail unrelated to athlete selection or power
Baseline strength associated with supplement choice and power
explanation: A confounder is related to both the exposure and outcome and can distort their observed association.

text: Rehabilitation records suggest intensive treatment speeds recovery, but severe injuries receive different programmes and recover slowly. What may confound the association?
options: Random error unrelated to rehabilitation intensity or recovery
An outcome definition chosen after observing recovery times
A report feature unrelated to injury severity, programme, or recovery
Initial injury severity associated with intensity and recovery time
explanation: A confounder is related to both the exposure and outcome and can distort their observed association.

text: Athletes attending altitude camps improve more, but fitter athletes are more likely to attend. What is the confounder?
options: Random error unrelated to camp choice and performance
An outcome definition selected after observing performance gains
Baseline fitness linked to camp selection and performance
A report feature unrelated to fitness or camp attendance
explanation: A confounder is related to both the exposure and outcome and can distort their observed association.

text: A screening score predicts injury, but previously injured athletes score poorly and are more likely to re-injure. What may confound the association?
options: Random error unrelated to screening score and reinjury
An outcome definition chosen after seeing the reinjury results
Previous injury associated with screening score and reinjury
A report feature unrelated to screening or reinjury
explanation: A confounder is related to both the exposure and outcome and can distort their observed association.

text: For an athlete entering a new training block, research involving athletes should include safeguards for:
options: Faster data collection without addressing participant risk
Consent, privacy, risk minimization, and fair treatment
Public release of identifiable health information
Exclusion of participant questions from consent discussions
explanation: Ethical research respects autonomy, confidentiality, safety, and fair participation.

text: An online study stores athlete names with GPS tracks and injury records. Which safeguard is most appropriate?
options: Code records, restrict access, obtain consent
Publish raw data so participants can verify records
Give all staff and sponsors unrestricted access
Explain the study only after collecting the data
explanation: Identifiable athlete data require informed consent, privacy safeguards, controlled access, and a clear explanation of how the information will be used.

text: A study recruits adolescent athletes for a fatigue-monitoring protocol. Ethical safeguards should include:
options: Obtain assent, parental consent, and a risk plan
Exclude questions to prevent misunderstanding
Publish individual scores to encourage compliance
Tie participation to team selection for full attendance
explanation: Research with young athletes requires appropriate consent and assent processes, risk oversight, and protection from coercion or unmanaged adverse events.

text: An athlete employed by the team is invited to join a study led by the head coach. To protect voluntary participation, the research team should:
options: Make participation mandatory for team selection
Use independent consent, explain risks, protect privacy
Collect verbal consent publicly in front of teammates
Explain the study only after all data collection
explanation: A power relationship can create undue influence; independent consent, transparent risk communication, confidentiality, and freedom to decline are essential.

text: Before collecting blood from youth athletes for a study, what is the key safeguard?
options: Obtain age-appropriate consent, reduce risk, and protect privacy
Publish identifiable records so results can be verified
Limit consent information to the coach's preferred questions
Collect samples before explaining study risks or discomfort
explanation: Ethical athlete research protects autonomy, privacy, welfare, voluntary participation, risk minimization, and fair treatment.

text: Before retaining GPS and wellness records for future club studies, what should the protocol ensure?
options: Store records before explaining future use, access, or privacy
Specify future-use consent, restrict access, and protect records
Exclude future-use questions to keep monitoring brief
Make identifiable records available to all performance staff
explanation: Ethical athlete research protects autonomy, privacy, welfare, voluntary participation, risk minimization, and fair treatment.

text: A lactate study involves brief discomfort and includes a control group. What safeguards are required?
options: Collect samples without discussing discomfort, alternatives, or risks
Explain discomfort, obtain voluntary consent, and monitor safety
Let the coach answer consent questions for the participant
Release individual lactate results to the squad without permission
explanation: Ethical athlete research protects autonomy, privacy, welfare, voluntary participation, risk minimization, and fair treatment.

text: A trial compares two conditioning programmes with no known superior option. What makes the protocol fair?
options: Use fair allocation, consent, risk oversight, and withdrawal rights
Reveal group allocation publicly to monitor adherence and compliance
Exclude withdrawal requests after the programme begins or changes
Assign athletes without explaining risks because programmes are equivalent
explanation: Ethical athlete research protects autonomy, privacy, welfare, voluntary participation, risk minimization, and fair treatment.

text: Before video-recording identifiable landing mechanics for publication, what must researchers do?
options: Obtain consent for identifiable video, publication, storage, and use
Post identifiable video publicly for transparent science without consent
Explain the recording only to the coach and not the participant
Record first and ask permission only if selected for publication
explanation: Ethical athlete research protects autonomy, privacy, welfare, voluntary participation, risk minimization, and fair treatment.

text: If participation in a monitoring study is linked to team selection, what is the ethical response?
options: Collect data before explaining selection-related risks, privacy, or voluntary refusal
Publish individual responses so selection appears transparent to the whole squad
Let the coach answer consent questions and discourage athletes from refusing
Separate research from selection; protect confidentiality and allow refusal
explanation: Ethical athlete research protects autonomy, privacy, welfare, voluntary participation, risk minimization, and fair treatment.
